With regard to the notorious plot to murder Gaius Caesar—I mean the Caesar who conquered Pompey and got control of the state—Tillius Cimber was trusted with it no less than Gaius Cassius. Now Cassius throughout his life drank water; while Tillius Cimber was a sot as well as a brawler. Cimber himself alluded to this fact, saying: "I carry a master? I cannot carry my liquor!" So let each one call to mind those who, to his knowledge, can be ill trusted with wine, but well trusted with the spoken word; and yet one case occurs to my mind, which I shall relate, lest it fall into oblivion. For life should be provided with conspicuous illustrations. Let us not always be harking back to the dim past.

Lucius Piso, the Director of Public Safety at Rome, was drunk from the very time of his appointment. He used to spend the greater part of the night at banquets, and would sleep until noon. That was the way he spent his morning hours. Nevertheless, he applied himself most diligently to his official duties, which included the guardianship of the city. Even the sainted Augustus trusted him with secret orders when he placed him in command of Thrace. Piso conquered that country. Tiberius, too, trusted him when he took his holiday in Campania, leaving behind him in the city many a critical matter that aroused both suspicion and hatred. I fancy that it was because Piso’s drunkenness turned out well for the Emperor that he appointed to the office of city prefect Cossus, a man of authority and balance, but so soaked and steeped in drink that once, at a meeting of the Senate, whither he had come after banqueting, he was overcome by a slumber from which he could not be roused, and had to be carried home. ### ARAB INFLUENCE IN SPAIN.

"There is a striking degree of similarity between many of the airs which I have heard in Egypt and some of the popular melodies of Spain." (Lane, "Modern Egyptians.") "Not only do we meet with certain terms and expressions in the popular songs of Spain," says Engel in his "Study of National Music," "which forcibly remind us of Arabic music, but also several Spanish instruments are of Arabic origin."

# III THE BULL-DIONYSUS

The representation of wood-spirits in goat-form appears to be both widespread and, to the primitive mind, natural. Therefore, when we find that Dionysus—a tree-god—is sometimes represented in goat form, we can hardly avoid the conclusion that this representation is simply part of his character as a tree-god, rather than a fusion of two independent cults—one a tree-god cult and the other a goat-god cult. If such a fusion occurred for Dionysus, it must also have occurred for the Pans and Satyrs of Greece, the Fauns of Italy, and the *Ljeschie* of Russia. That such a fusion of disconnected cults occurred once is possible; that it occurred twice independently is improbable; and that it occurred three times is practically incredible.

Dionysus was also represented, as we have seen, in the form of a bull. We are led to expect that his bull form is just another expression of his character as a vegetation deity, especially since the bull is a common embodiment of the corn-spirit in Northern Europe, and his association with Demeter and Proserpine at Eleusis shows he had strong agricultural affinities. The only other possible explanation is that the bull-conception was originally distinct and was merged due to something like the union of two tribes (a view suggested by Mr. Andrew Lang).

When a competent number have passed through a sufficient trial of their faith in the junior order, and are unitedly prepared to establish and support Church relation, they have only to ratify and confirm their inward agreement by executing what is, by way of eminence, called the Church Covenant. *Festivals.* There is no act of uniformity and no ecclesiastical calendar regulating the festivals or forms of worship of village deities, and no universal custom as to the appointment of ministrants. In some villages, where there is a permanent shrine, offerings of rice, fruit, and flowers, with incense and camphor, are made every day by the villagers who have made vows to the goddess, through the pūjārī . Often offerings are made once or twice a week, on fixed days, consisting chiefly of grain, fruit, and flowers, and occasionally of goats, sheep, and fowls. In many places there is a fixed annual festival, which sometimes takes place after harvest when the people are at leisure and have plenty of food; but there is no regular rule as to the time, and the custom varies widely in different districts. In most places, however, there is no regular annual festival, but sacrifices are offered whenever an epidemic or any other calamity occurs which may make it expedient to propitiate the goddess. In some villages, old men complained to me that whereas formerly sacrifices were offered yearly, now, owing to the decay of religion, they are only offered once in four or five years. So, again, there is no uniformity as to the duration of a festival. Generally it lasts about a week, but in the Tamil country it is sometimes a very elaborate affair, lasting for a fortnight, three weeks, or even a whole month; so too in some parts of the Canarese country, the Māri festival, which is held in February, lasts for about four weeks. But a long festival is an expensive luxury that only a large town or a well-to-do village is able to afford. Speaking generally, the object of the festival is simply to propitiate the goddess.

Every village in South India is believed by the people to be surrounded by evil spirits, who are always on the watch to inflict diseases and misfortunes of all kinds on the unhappy villagers. They lurk everywhere—on the tops of palmyra trees, in caves and rocks, in ravines and chasms. They fly about in the air like birds of prey, ready to pounce down upon any unprotected victim, and the Indian villagers pass through life in constant dread of these invisible enemies. Consequently, the poor people turn for protection to the guardian deities of their village. It is the function of these deities to ward off evil spirits and protect the village from epidemics of cholera, smallpox, or fever, as well as from cattle disease, failure of crops, childlessness, fires, and all the manifold ills that human life is subject to in an Indian village.

The sole object, then, of the worship of these village deities is to appease them and to avert their wrath. There is no idea of praise and thanksgiving, no expression of gratitude or love, and no desire for any spiritual or moral blessings. The one objective is to get rid of cholera, smallpox, cattle disease, or drought, or to avert some of the minor evils of life. The worship, therefore, in most of the villages, only takes place occasionally. Sometimes, as I have stated above, daily offerings are made to the deity; but, as a rule, the worship is confined to one large sacrifice, which takes place once a year, or on the occasion of some special disaster or outbreak of disease. The general attitude of the villager towards his village deity is “Let sleeping dogs lie.” So long as everything goes well, and there is no disease afflicting man or beast, and no drought nor other great calamity, it seems safest to leave the goddess alone. But when misfortune comes, it is a sign that she is out of temper, and it is time to take steps to appease her wrath.

"Difficult are the things that are beautiful," said Solon. Plato asserted that goodness accompanies difficulty. But Aristotle, Prince and Leader of philosophers, testified that virtue and art reside in difficult things. Indeed, it is true; thus, while the art and science of Medicine is most beautiful, it exists as a difficult thing, which, however, goodness and utility accompany: such as health itself, peace of mind, and among the wise, the highest honor. Moved and stirred by these things, the most august Emperors of the Romans, the most invincible Kings, and the highest Pontiffs of our ages, delighted greatly in this study. For that Augustus Caesar gladly used a medical composition invented by himself, which later many Physicians translated into their own books. Nero, that tyrant and indeed unpraised, yet truly most learned, is said to have placed a part of his study in this genre. Tiberius Caesar, according to Galen, composed troches for shingles. The antidotes of Adrian and Justinian are celebrated to this very day. Avicenna, Prince of the Arabs, in the remedies written by himself, praises the testimony of King Chabit in several places. In the commentaries of Serapis, Iacibusa, King of the Medes, and likewise King Chemur, are counted as witnesses of Medicine. I pass over Juba, King of Mauretania, who adorned the herb named Euphorbia with wonderful praises. I pass over Lysimachus, Gentius, and Eupator, Kings not ignorant of the medical art, who left their own names given to plants to be remembered for an eternal age. I pass over that one of Phoebus...

## CHAPTER VI.

### *History of Typhon.*

Diodorus makes Typhon born of the Titans. Plutarch says he is the brother of Osiris and Isis: some others advance that he was born from the Earth, when Juno irritated struck it with her foot; that the fear he had of Jupiter made him flee to Egypt, where, unable to endure the heat of the climate, he threw himself into a lake where he perished. Hesiod gives us a most atrocious depiction of him , which Apollodorus seems to have copied. The Earth, they say, outraged with fury that Jupiter had struck the Titans with his thunderbolts, joined with Tartarus, and making one last effort, she gave birth to Typhon. This dreadful monster had a greatness and a strength superior to all the others combined. His height was so enormous that he far surpassed the highest mountains, and his head penetrated to the stars. His extended arms reached from the orient to the occident, and from his hands came one hundred furious dragons,

Attempts have been made to explain what the ancient authors said about Typhon morally, historically, and physically. The applications that have been made of it have sometimes been quite successful; but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within the same system.
